medical.title: Study reveals how congenital anomalies and deprivation impact children's educational achievement
medical.summary: New Welsh research has revealed how the combination of congenital anomalies, socioeconomic deprivation and other aspects of children's health and educational circumstances influences their attainment.

medical.title: Platelets may play an unexpected role in glioblastoma progression
medical.summary: New Cleveland Clinic research published in Cancer Cell shows that people with glioblastoma have more active platelets, which are cells involved in blood clotting. Platelets also communicate with other cells and can influence immune activity. The overactive platelets in people with glioblastoma slow the activity of cancer-fighting T cells, which can contribute to tumor growth and cancer progression.

medical.title: Alcohol use held steady among cancer survivors
medical.summary: The drinking rate of adults who have had cancer has remained unchanged for nearly a decade, according to a new study by researchers at the WashU Brown School.

medical.title: Beyond treating symptoms: Life stories support mental health recovery
medical.summary: UT research shows how personal life stories can support treatment and personal recovery. Who are you, what has shaped you, and how do you see your future? For people with personality disorders, these questions can play an important role in their recovery. Ph.D. research by clinical psychologist and psychotherapist Silvia Pol shows that paying attention to personal life stories can help guide treatment decisions and support personal recovery.

medical.title: Safer solutions: The urgent connection between smoking and HIV
medical.summary: People with HIV now lose more years of life to smoking than to HIV itself. About 1.2 million Americans are living with HIV, and while smoking among U.S. adults has fallen below 10% for the first time, people with HIV still smoke at up to four times that rate. Although many people with HIV want to quit smoking, their quit rates are much lower compared to the general population.

medical.title: CDK1 protein offers clues to which breast cancers will resist targeted therapy
medical.summary: Researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have discovered that the activity of a protein called CDK1 in breast cancers is linked to how they respond to a common therapy—an insight that could inform more personalized treatment approaches for patients.

medical.title: Hospitalized medical patients may fare better when treated by female physicians, study finds
medical.summary: Patients cared for by female physicians in the hospital were less likely to die or be readmitted than those treated by male physicians, according to a new ICES study led by a University of Toronto researcher. This suggests that care by female physicians may be associated with better short- and long-term outcomes among patients hospitalized with common medical diagnoses.

medical.title: One in four Americans have exaggerated or made up symptoms to try to get antibiotics
medical.summary: More than a quarter of Americans have exaggerated or made up symptoms to try to get antibiotics from their doctor, either for themselves or for their children, a new study has found. The survey of nearly 1,000 people nationwide uncovered common motivations for misrepresenting symptoms, including feeling very sick or needing to return to work or school.

medical.title: Music paired with beats may cut stress hormone more than twice as much as pink noise
medical.summary: A new randomized clinical trial from Toronto Metropolitan University (TMU) found that listening to just 24 minutes of personalized music paired with auditory beat stimulation (ABS) lowered levels of the stress hormone cortisol more than twice as much as pink noise, a popular sound used for relaxation. Yet participants reported feeling equally calm after both.

medical.title: Vegans may have less diverse gut bacteria, with lower protein intake offering possible clue
medical.summary: The gut is home to billions of microorganisms. It is a complex ecosystem that regulates many of the body's functions and helps keep us healthy—when it is in balance. Our diet influences this ecosystem. But does it matter whether a person is vegan or omnivorous?

medical.title: Review finds no evidence that testosterone improves brain fog during menopause
medical.summary: There is not enough evidence to determine whether testosterone helps with thinking and memory in midlife women, even though it is often prescribed in the UK, according to a UCL study.

medical.title: Study participants tricked into feeling an extra finger experience altered perceptions of their hand's abilities
medical.summary: The brain can sometimes trick itself into feeling like it has an extra appendage or that the body extends farther into space than it actually does. This can happen when signals in the brain get crossed due to a mix of visual and tactile cues in the environment. This phenomenon has been the subject of several studies. Now, a study published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance goes a step beyond making the brain think it has an extra part to testing if this also reshapes the perception of the body's capabilities.

medical.title: Brain circuit helps mothers wake up when their pups call
medical.summary: For many new mothers, sleeping uninterruptedly every night is challenging or unfeasible. One reason for this is that their newborn's crying can easily wake them, even when another caregiver is present and could tend to their babies.

medical.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
medical.summary: A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care.

medical.title: Cold shower routine may reduce sick days while cutting carbon emissions
medical.summary: How can we encourage people to adopt more environmentally friendly habits? To explore this question, a psychologist asked participants in a study to take cold showers. Those who stuck with the routine experienced several benefits.

medical.title: Halloween is typically a massive candy fest for kids—but it doesn't have to be
medical.summary: Halloween can be a massive candy fest. Children come home from trick-or-treating ready to dig into a sackful of candy and chocolate bars.

medical.title: How does daylight saving time affect our health?
medical.summary: The chicken or the egg? Cats or dogs? What about pineapple on pizza?

medical.title: A new framework for safe, patient-centered prescribing of obesity medications in older adults
medical.summary: The American Geriatrics Society (AGS) has released a new framework to assist clinicians in safely prescribing obesity medications in older adults. Organized around a series of cases, the framework offers a practical approach to prescribing obesity medications to older adults, including GLP-1 medications that act through gut-derived hormonal pathways.

medical.title: Cholesterol-sharing mechanism points to potential new target for pancreatic cancer treatment
medical.summary: Fox Chase Cancer Center researchers identified a potential therapeutic target for pancreatic cancer after showing that tumor growth can be slowed and immune suppression can be reduced in preclinical trials by blocking a particular protein, called anoctamin 6 (ANO6).

medical.title: Nursing decisions to navigate when dying patients become unresponsive
medical.summary: Flinders University research published in the Journal of Advanced Nursing has examined how specialist palliative care nurses navigate these complex decisions and found they draw on clinical expertise, ethical judgment, close observation and family engagement to guide care during a patient's final days.

medical.title: Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
medical.summary: A major new study reveals that drinking just two alcoholic beverages a day is associated with a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of death from alcohol-related causes, challenging the idea that moderate drinking is harmless. Researchers also found no significant overall health benefits from alcohol, with risks rising as consumption increases.

medical.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
medical.summary: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

medical.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
medical.summary: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.

medical.title: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
medical.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage.

medical.title: The new certification scheme helping solar farms become havens for wildlife
medical.summary: A new solar certification scheme encourages developers to create better habitats for wildlife alongside clean electricity generation The post The new certification scheme helping solar farms become havens for wildlife appeared first on Positive News .

science.title: How fish schools swim in sync may come down to following one influential neighbor
science.summary: Fish schools are a marvel of navigation. They move in concert without any one fish leading the way. Instead, their coordinated movements arise from individual fish continually adjusting their movements based on their neighbors. But how much of this social information each fish processes at once is less well understood.

science.title: Global change may alter how ocellated lizards move between shelters, food and predators
science.summary: Global change is also affecting the behavior and mobility of the ocellated lizard, a reptile typical of Mediterranean ecosystems. This species—the largest lizard on the Iberian Peninsula—could experience changes in its ability to move efficiently between shelters and feeding areas, escape predators and interact with its natural environment. This is the conclusion of a paper published in the Journal of Animal Ecology led by researcher Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou, from the Faculty of Biology and the Biodiversity Research Institute (IRBio) at the University of Barcelona.

science.title: Discovery of bromochloropyrene reveals unexpected biological properties
science.summary: Environmental pollutants containing chlorine or bromine have been widely studied, but compounds containing both elements have remained largely unexplored. Researchers have now detected bromochloropyrene in industrial soils and harbor sediments, investigated its breakdown under simulated sunlight, and measured its activity through a biological receptor linked to toxic effects. The findings reveal distinct environmental and biological properties, highlighting the need to investigate other mixed-halogen pollutants and improve future environmental monitoring and risk assessment.

science.title: Researchers create light-activated cages for 'protein killer' molecules
science.summary: Researchers have created a molecular "cage" that keeps protein-degrading drug molecules inactive until they are exposed to low-energy red light. The technology, called RuPHOTACs, controls when and where these molecules become active, which could help scientists develop treatments that destroy specific proteins while limiting unwanted effects elsewhere.

science.title: Grades are not comparable across schools in Sweden, says researcher
science.summary: Grades from compulsory school determine which pupils are accepted into popular upper secondary programs. A new thesis from Uppsala University shows that pupils at for-profit independent schools have, on average, higher grades than would statistically be expected given their backgrounds. The findings suggest that grading is more generous in independent schools and that the differences in grades may give pupils from high-income households a greater advantage in the competition for places at upper secondary school, at the expense of other pupils.

science.title: Quantum skyrmions outlast entanglement, hinting at more resilient networks
science.summary: Quantum networks could one day connect quantum computers into more powerful systems and enable new forms of secure communication. But a fundamental obstacle stands in the way: Quantum information is extraordinarily fragile, and the entanglement between particles of light on which such networks would depend is easily disrupted.

science.title: Scientists find that a 10-millisecond flash could help build more sensitive gas sensors
science.summary: Nitrogen dioxide is a harmful gas that requires sensitive detection. Researchers used intense light pulses lasting 10 milliseconds to make molybdenum disulfide flakes and anchor isolated metal atoms in one step. Adding platinum improved the material's room-temperature response to nitrogen dioxide, reaching 100.8% at 400 parts per billion and a detection limit of 17.2 parts per billion. This approach could support advanced gas sensors and applications in catalysis and energy technologies.

science.title: Personal stories offer new insights into stuttering therapy, researchers find
science.summary: Traditional speech-language therapy for people who stutter has largely operated under a medical model focused on eliminating dysfluency—breaks in the normal rhythm of speech. But for Rodney Gabel, a professor of speech-language pathology at Binghamton University, and Ladan Khoshbin, a doctoral student in Binghamton's Community Research and Action program, true progress in stuttering research begins with listening to people's stories.

science.title: Customizable nanoparticles show potential for delivering personalized cancer vaccines
science.summary: A nanoscale particle with a unique structure, developed at MIT, holds potential as a customizable delivery vehicle for personalized cancer vaccines. The backbone of the vaccine is a modified, harmless bacteriophage called M13, which forms a nanofiber that can be coated with cancer antigens. By precisely controlling the density of those cancer proteins, the researchers found that they could create a vaccine that prevents the development of colon tumors in mice.

science.title: NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope
science.summary: NASA issued a Request for Information Oct. 29 to learn more about industry capabilities for in-space servicing to support the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope.

science.title: New research challenges long-held beliefs about Robert Burns and Jamaica
science.summary: A new study by academics at the University of Glasgow provides the most detailed analysis to date of Robert Burns' connections with Jamaica and relationship to the Atlantic slavery system.

science.title: NASA's Voyager 1 conserves power, resolves brief communications pause
science.summary: NASA's Voyager team is celebrating two recent developments with the Voyager 1 spacecraft: In September, they successfully completed a months-long effort to stretch the spacecraft's diminishing power supply. Then, on Oct. 20, an unexpected loss of communication with the spacecraft resolved itself after 48 hours, before the team sent commands to the spacecraft to troubleshoot the issue.

science.title: The genetic cost of being a lazy parent ... if you're a cuckoo finch
science.summary: African cuckoo finches (Anomalospiza imberbis) are very deceptive birds, or at least the mothers are. They sneak into the nests of other birds, such as prinias and cisticolas, to lay their eggs, then slip away and leave the hosts to raise the chicks.

science.title: Marine fossils in Colombia reveal possible evolutionary transition without mass extinction
science.summary: A remarkably diverse fossil ecosystem in central Colombia that preserves an unusual overlap between survivors of older Jurassic groups and newer Cretaceous lineages has led researchers at McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) to recognize a new pattern of large-scale evolutionary transition, one that does not include mass extinctions.

science.title: JWST reveals a distant galaxy that may let most of its ionizing radiation escape
science.summary: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have found evidence that a distant, exceptionally blue galaxy may allow most of its ionizing radiation to escape into space. Known as EBG-1, the gravitationally lensed galaxy is seen at a redshift of 9.244, about 530 million years after the Big Bang. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 16.

science.title: NASA's TRACERS first results offer peek into violent magnetic process
science.summary: NASA's TRACERS (Tandem Reconnection and Cusp Electrodynamics Reconnaissance Satellites) mission has gathered its first clues to how space weather affects Earth's magnetic field. In a new paper published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics, researchers break down how these interactions work after analyzing initial observations from the first year of the mission.

science.title: WaterPuzzle uses magnets to model water's hydrogen bonds for hands-on classroom exploration
science.summary: Water is one of the most essential components of life, and many of its unique properties arise from interactions between its molecules. Hydrogen bonds influence water's physical properties, contribute to the formation of ice crystals and are crucial for normal biological processes. Understanding these interactions is fundamental to chemistry, physics and biology.

science.title: China's leading universities often pair leaders with complementary backgrounds, analysis of 132 pairs finds
science.summary: China's leading universities face two overlapping pressures: competing globally while remaining aligned with national strategic priorities. A study of 132 university president–party secretary pairs, conducted by a Hiroshima University researcher, found that 53% had different but potentially complementary backgrounds and experience, the most common of three leadership configurations.

science.title: Resident experience matters in estimating neighborhood walkability, study shows
science.summary: Walking has been shown to improve the overall health of a community and can predict the prevalence of chronic diseases, such as obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, according to the World Health Organization. Because of this, city planners assess neighborhoods' walkability, which measures how built environments support walking, when planning improvements.

science.title: Confirming altermagnetism: A geometric twist offers experimental proof
science.summary: For decades, physicists recognized only two types of magnetism that occur in materials without external influence: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. In findings published in Science, a team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory has delivered conclusive experimental proof of a third magnetic phase called altermagnetism.

science.title: Long-standing Indigenous practice of adding shells to sand helps young clams withstand ocean acidification
science.summary: New research from the University of California, Davis, reveals why adding crushed shells to beach sand helps protect shell-making animals—such as clams, oysters and mussels—from the detrimental effects of ocean acidification.

science.title: Burrowing shrimp are on the move in a mudflat near you
science.summary: Burrowing shrimp are a pest well known to shellfish growers. These pale-bodied creatures excavate mud as they dig into the ground, creating piles of sediment that suffocate oysters and clams growing on the surface. In estuaries on the West Coast, shrimp beds reach densities of hundreds of shrimp per square meter, but the boundaries of the beds change.

science.title: Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
science.summary: Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock.

science.title: Unusual quantum states in six-layer graphene offer clues to superconductivity
science.summary: Graphene, a material consisting of a sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern, has proved promising for various technological applications. Materials in which several layers of graphene are stacked together can exhibit different advantageous properties.

science.title: Asking teachers to set high expectations leads to more detailed feedback and reveals subtle bias, study finds
science.summary: Prompting teachers to communicate high expectations and confidence in students' potential leads them to give more detailed feedback, according to a new study led by Yasemin Copur-Gencturk, Ph.D., a professor of education at USC Rossier and co-director of the USC STEM Center; Ian Thacker, Ph.D., an associate professor of educational psychology at The University of Texas at San Antonio; and Joseph Cimpian, Ph.D., a professor of economics and education policy at New York University.

environment.title: Suriname’s rich archaeological history may hold keys to conservation
environment.summary: Suriname pledges to save its forests but neglects the ancient human history hidden within them, experts say.

Centered in Guildford, Surrey, its rolling fields pop with wildflowers in the spring; birds sing and ducks paddle serenely in a pond beside ornamental gardens; and the sun casts dappled shade on the grass from oak, spruce and beech trees, scattered across 52 hectares […]

Soundscape ecology rests on a simple conviction: the collective voices of the nonhuman world are not only eloquent, but essential. Recorded and preserved over time, […]

The nonprofit Conservation Lands Foundation (CLF) recently catalogued 12 such policy actions in its newly released Public Lands […]

environment.summary: KAKINADA, India (AP) — A powerful cyclone battered India ’s Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday, killing at least three people and damaging homes and farmland after authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people, officials said. environment.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
environment.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
environment.summary: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.

environment.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
environment.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

environment.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
environment.summary: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

environment.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
environment.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

environment.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
environment.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.

mix_items.summary: Active digitale în valoare de aproximativ 6,3 miliarde de dolari au fost transferate joi seară din portofelele Binance, în urma unui atac cibernetic care s-a desfășurat, în mare parte, în numai 20 de minute. mix_items.title: How fish schools swim in sync may come down to following one influential neighbor
mix_items.summary: Fish schools are a marvel of navigation. They move in concert without any one fish leading the way. Instead, their coordinated movements arise from individual fish continually adjusting their movements based on their neighbors. But how much of this social information each fish processes at once is less well understood.

mix_items.summary: New Welsh research has revealed how the combination of congenital anomalies, socioeconomic deprivation and other aspects of children's health and educational circumstances influences their attainment.

mix_items.title: Global change may alter how ocellated lizards move between shelters, food and predators
mix_items.summary: Global change is also affecting the behavior and mobility of the ocellated lizard, a reptile typical of Mediterranean ecosystems. This species—the largest lizard on the Iberian Peninsula—could experience changes in its ability to move efficiently between shelters and feeding areas, escape predators and interact with its natural environment. This is the conclusion of a paper published in the Journal of Animal Ecology led by researcher Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou, from the Faculty of Biology and the Biodiversity Research Institute (IRBio) at the University of Barcelona.

mix_items.title: Platelets may play an unexpected role in glioblastoma progression
mix_items.summary: New Cleveland Clinic research published in Cancer Cell shows that people with glioblastoma have more active platelets, which are cells involved in blood clotting. Platelets also communicate with other cells and can influence immune activity. The overactive platelets in people with glioblastoma slow the activity of cancer-fighting T cells, which can contribute to tumor growth and cancer progression.

mix_items.title: Alcohol use held steady among cancer survivors
mix_items.summary: The drinking rate of adults who have had cancer has remained unchanged for nearly a decade, according to a new study by researchers at the WashU Brown School.

mix_items.title: Discovery of bromochloropyrene reveals unexpected biological properties
mix_items.summary: Environmental pollutants containing chlorine or bromine have been widely studied, but compounds containing both elements have remained largely unexplored. Researchers have now detected bromochloropyrene in industrial soils and harbor sediments, investigated its breakdown under simulated sunlight, and measured its activity through a biological receptor linked to toxic effects. The findings reveal distinct environmental and biological properties, highlighting the need to investigate other mixed-halogen pollutants and improve future environmental monitoring and risk assessment.

mix_items.title: Researchers create light-activated cages for 'protein killer' molecules
mix_items.summary: Researchers have created a molecular "cage" that keeps protein-degrading drug molecules inactive until they are exposed to low-energy red light. The technology, called RuPHOTACs, controls when and where these molecules become active, which could help scientists develop treatments that destroy specific proteins while limiting unwanted effects elsewhere.

mix_items.title: Grades are not comparable across schools in Sweden, says researcher
mix_items.summary: Grades from compulsory school determine which pupils are accepted into popular upper secondary programs. A new thesis from Uppsala University shows that pupils at for-profit independent schools have, on average, higher grades than would statistically be expected given their backgrounds. The findings suggest that grading is more generous in independent schools and that the differences in grades may give pupils from high-income households a greater advantage in the competition for places at upper secondary school, at the expense of other pupils.

mix_items.title: Beyond treating symptoms: Life stories support mental health recovery
mix_items.summary: UT research shows how personal life stories can support treatment and personal recovery. Who are you, what has shaped you, and how do you see your future? For people with personality disorders, these questions can play an important role in their recovery. Ph.D. research by clinical psychologist and psychotherapist Silvia Pol shows that paying attention to personal life stories can help guide treatment decisions and support personal recovery.

mix_items.title: Quantum skyrmions outlast entanglement, hinting at more resilient networks
mix_items.summary: Quantum networks could one day connect quantum computers into more powerful systems and enable new forms of secure communication. But a fundamental obstacle stands in the way: Quantum information is extraordinarily fragile, and the entanglement between particles of light on which such networks would depend is easily disrupted.

mix_items.title: Safer solutions: The urgent connection between smoking and HIV
mix_items.summary: People with HIV now lose more years of life to smoking than to HIV itself. About 1.2 million Americans are living with HIV, and while smoking among U.S. adults has fallen below 10% for the first time, people with HIV still smoke at up to four times that rate. Although many people with HIV want to quit smoking, their quit rates are much lower compared to the general population.

mix_items.title: Scientists find that a 10-millisecond flash could help build more sensitive gas sensors
mix_items.summary: Nitrogen dioxide is a harmful gas that requires sensitive detection. Researchers used intense light pulses lasting 10 milliseconds to make molybdenum disulfide flakes and anchor isolated metal atoms in one step. Adding platinum improved the material's room-temperature response to nitrogen dioxide, reaching 100.8% at 400 parts per billion and a detection limit of 17.2 parts per billion. This approach could support advanced gas sensors and applications in catalysis and energy technologies.

mix_items.title: CDK1 protein offers clues to which breast cancers will resist targeted therapy
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have discovered that the activity of a protein called CDK1 in breast cancers is linked to how they respond to a common therapy—an insight that could inform more personalized treatment approaches for patients.

mix_items.title: Personal stories offer new insights into stuttering therapy, researchers find
mix_items.summary: Traditional speech-language therapy for people who stutter has largely operated under a medical model focused on eliminating dysfluency—breaks in the normal rhythm of speech. But for Rodney Gabel, a professor of speech-language pathology at Binghamton University, and Ladan Khoshbin, a doctoral student in Binghamton's Community Research and Action program, true progress in stuttering research begins with listening to people's stories.

mix_items.title: Customizable nanoparticles show potential for delivering personalized cancer vaccines
mix_items.summary: A nanoscale particle with a unique structure, developed at MIT, holds potential as a customizable delivery vehicle for personalized cancer vaccines. The backbone of the vaccine is a modified, harmless bacteriophage called M13, which forms a nanofiber that can be coated with cancer antigens. By precisely controlling the density of those cancer proteins, the researchers found that they could create a vaccine that prevents the development of colon tumors in mice.

mix_items.title: Hospitalized medical patients may fare better when treated by female physicians, study finds
mix_items.summary: Patients cared for by female physicians in the hospital were less likely to die or be readmitted than those treated by male physicians, according to a new ICES study led by a University of Toronto researcher. This suggests that care by female physicians may be associated with better short- and long-term outcomes among patients hospitalized with common medical diagnoses.

mix_items.title: One in four Americans have exaggerated or made up symptoms to try to get antibiotics
mix_items.summary: More than a quarter of Americans have exaggerated or made up symptoms to try to get antibiotics from their doctor, either for themselves or for their children, a new study has found. The survey of nearly 1,000 people nationwide uncovered common motivations for misrepresenting symptoms, including feeling very sick or needing to return to work or school.

mix_items.title: NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope
mix_items.summary: NASA issued a Request for Information Oct. 29 to learn more about industry capabilities for in-space servicing to support the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope.

mix_items.title: New research challenges long-held beliefs about Robert Burns and Jamaica
mix_items.summary: A new study by academics at the University of Glasgow provides the most detailed analysis to date of Robert Burns' connections with Jamaica and relationship to the Atlantic slavery system.

mix_items.title: NASA's Voyager 1 conserves power, resolves brief communications pause
mix_items.summary: NASA's Voyager team is celebrating two recent developments with the Voyager 1 spacecraft: In September, they successfully completed a months-long effort to stretch the spacecraft's diminishing power supply. Then, on Oct. 20, an unexpected loss of communication with the spacecraft resolved itself after 48 hours, before the team sent commands to the spacecraft to troubleshoot the issue.

mix_items.title: The genetic cost of being a lazy parent ... if you're a cuckoo finch
mix_items.summary: African cuckoo finches (Anomalospiza imberbis) are very deceptive birds, or at least the mothers are. They sneak into the nests of other birds, such as prinias and cisticolas, to lay their eggs, then slip away and leave the hosts to raise the chicks.

mix_items.title: Music paired with beats may cut stress hormone more than twice as much as pink noise
mix_items.summary: A new randomized clinical trial from Toronto Metropolitan University (TMU) found that listening to just 24 minutes of personalized music paired with auditory beat stimulation (ABS) lowered levels of the stress hormone cortisol more than twice as much as pink noise, a popular sound used for relaxation. Yet participants reported feeling equally calm after both.

mix_items.title: Vegans may have less diverse gut bacteria, with lower protein intake offering possible clue
mix_items.summary: The gut is home to billions of microorganisms. It is a complex ecosystem that regulates many of the body's functions and helps keep us healthy—when it is in balance. Our diet influences this ecosystem. But does it matter whether a person is vegan or omnivorous?

mix_items.title: Marine fossils in Colombia reveal possible evolutionary transition without mass extinction
mix_items.summary: A remarkably diverse fossil ecosystem in central Colombia that preserves an unusual overlap between survivors of older Jurassic groups and newer Cretaceous lineages has led researchers at McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) to recognize a new pattern of large-scale evolutionary transition, one that does not include mass extinctions.

mix_items.title: JWST reveals a distant galaxy that may let most of its ionizing radiation escape
mix_items.summary: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have found evidence that a distant, exceptionally blue galaxy may allow most of its ionizing radiation to escape into space. Known as EBG-1, the gravitationally lensed galaxy is seen at a redshift of 9.244, about 530 million years after the Big Bang. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 16.

mix_items.title: NASA's TRACERS first results offer peek into violent magnetic process
mix_items.summary: NASA's TRACERS (Tandem Reconnection and Cusp Electrodynamics Reconnaissance Satellites) mission has gathered its first clues to how space weather affects Earth's magnetic field. In a new paper published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics, researchers break down how these interactions work after analyzing initial observations from the first year of the mission.

mix_items.title: Review finds no evidence that testosterone improves brain fog during menopause
mix_items.summary: There is not enough evidence to determine whether testosterone helps with thinking and memory in midlife women, even though it is often prescribed in the UK, according to a UCL study.

mix_items.title: WaterPuzzle uses magnets to model water's hydrogen bonds for hands-on classroom exploration
mix_items.summary: Water is one of the most essential components of life, and many of its unique properties arise from interactions between its molecules. Hydrogen bonds influence water's physical properties, contribute to the formation of ice crystals and are crucial for normal biological processes. Understanding these interactions is fundamental to chemistry, physics and biology.

mix_items.title: Study participants tricked into feeling an extra finger experience altered perceptions of their hand's abilities
mix_items.summary: The brain can sometimes trick itself into feeling like it has an extra appendage or that the body extends farther into space than it actually does. This can happen when signals in the brain get crossed due to a mix of visual and tactile cues in the environment. This phenomenon has been the subject of several studies. Now, a study published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance goes a step beyond making the brain think it has an extra part to testing if this also reshapes the perception of the body's capabilities.

mix_items.title: China's leading universities often pair leaders with complementary backgrounds, analysis of 132 pairs finds
mix_items.summary: China's leading universities face two overlapping pressures: competing globally while remaining aligned with national strategic priorities. A study of 132 university president–party secretary pairs, conducted by a Hiroshima University researcher, found that 53% had different but potentially complementary backgrounds and experience, the most common of three leadership configurations.

mix_items.title: Resident experience matters in estimating neighborhood walkability, study shows
mix_items.summary: Walking has been shown to improve the overall health of a community and can predict the prevalence of chronic diseases, such as obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, according to the World Health Organization. Because of this, city planners assess neighborhoods' walkability, which measures how built environments support walking, when planning improvements.

mix_items.title: Brain circuit helps mothers wake up when their pups call
mix_items.summary: For many new mothers, sleeping uninterruptedly every night is challenging or unfeasible. One reason for this is that their newborn's crying can easily wake them, even when another caregiver is present and could tend to their babies.

mix_items.title: Confirming altermagnetism: A geometric twist offers experimental proof
mix_items.summary: For decades, physicists recognized only two types of magnetism that occur in materials without external influence: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. In findings published in Science, a team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory has delivered conclusive experimental proof of a third magnetic phase called altermagnetism.

mix_items.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
mix_items.summary: A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care.

mix_items.title: Long-standing Indigenous practice of adding shells to sand helps young clams withstand ocean acidification
mix_items.summary: New research from the University of California, Davis, reveals why adding crushed shells to beach sand helps protect shell-making animals—such as clams, oysters and mussels—from the detrimental effects of ocean acidification.

mix_items.title: Burrowing shrimp are on the move in a mudflat near you
mix_items.summary: Burrowing shrimp are a pest well known to shellfish growers. These pale-bodied creatures excavate mud as they dig into the ground, creating piles of sediment that suffocate oysters and clams growing on the surface. In estuaries on the West Coast, shrimp beds reach densities of hundreds of shrimp per square meter, but the boundaries of the beds change.

mix_items.title: Cold shower routine may reduce sick days while cutting carbon emissions
mix_items.summary: How can we encourage people to adopt more environmentally friendly habits? To explore this question, a psychologist asked participants in a study to take cold showers. Those who stuck with the routine experienced several benefits.

mix_items.title: Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock.

mix_items.title: Halloween is typically a massive candy fest for kids—but it doesn't have to be
mix_items.summary: Halloween can be a massive candy fest. Children come home from trick-or-treating ready to dig into a sackful of candy and chocolate bars.

mix_items.title: Unusual quantum states in six-layer graphene offer clues to superconductivity
mix_items.summary: Graphene, a material consisting of a sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern, has proved promising for various technological applications. Materials in which several layers of graphene are stacked together can exhibit different advantageous properties.

mix_items.title: Asking teachers to set high expectations leads to more detailed feedback and reveals subtle bias, study finds
mix_items.summary: Prompting teachers to communicate high expectations and confidence in students' potential leads them to give more detailed feedback, according to a new study led by Yasemin Copur-Gencturk, Ph.D., a professor of education at USC Rossier and co-director of the USC STEM Center; Ian Thacker, Ph.D., an associate professor of educational psychology at The University of Texas at San Antonio; and Joseph Cimpian, Ph.D., a professor of economics and education policy at New York University.

mix_items.title: How does daylight saving time affect our health?
mix_items.summary: The chicken or the egg? Cats or dogs? What about pineapple on pizza?

mix_items.title: A new framework for safe, patient-centered prescribing of obesity medications in older adults
mix_items.summary: The American Geriatrics Society (AGS) has released a new framework to assist clinicians in safely prescribing obesity medications in older adults. Organized around a series of cases, the framework offers a practical approach to prescribing obesity medications to older adults, including GLP-1 medications that act through gut-derived hormonal pathways.

mix_items.title: Cholesterol-sharing mechanism points to potential new target for pancreatic cancer treatment
mix_items.summary: Fox Chase Cancer Center researchers identified a potential therapeutic target for pancreatic cancer after showing that tumor growth can be slowed and immune suppression can be reduced in preclinical trials by blocking a particular protein, called anoctamin 6 (ANO6).

mix_items.title: Nursing decisions to navigate when dying patients become unresponsive
mix_items.summary: Flinders University research published in the Journal of Advanced Nursing has examined how specialist palliative care nurses navigate these complex decisions and found they draw on clinical expertise, ethical judgment, close observation and family engagement to guide care during a patient's final days.

mix_items.title: Suriname’s rich archaeological history may hold keys to conservation
mix_items.summary: Suriname pledges to save its forests but neglects the ancient human history hidden within them, experts say.

mix_items.title: A town-wide ‘living laboratory’ shows how green spaces can combat climate extremes
mix_items.summary: Stoke Park is a natural haven in a busy British town. Centered in Guildford, Surrey, its rolling fields pop with wildflowers in the spring; birds sing and ducks paddle serenely in a pond beside ornamental gardens; and the sun casts dappled shade on the grass from oak, spruce and beech trees, scattered across 52 hectares […]

mix_items.title: Why I sent my archive of nature’s sounds to France (commentary)
mix_items.summary: It is a peculiar irony: as technology reaches ever deeper into Earth’s living systems, the primal sonic expressions of the natural world—wind, water, leaf, and creature—have never been more imperiled. Soundscape ecology rests on a simple conviction: the collective voices of the nonhuman world are not only eloquent, but essential. Recorded and preserved over time, […]

mix_items.title: US public lands tracker highlights the collective impact of Trump policies
mix_items.summary: In his second term as the U.S. president, Donald Trump has taken actions to remove protections from at least 34.8 million hectares (86 million acres) of public lands, according to the advocacy group Center for American Progress. The nonprofit Conservation Lands Foundation (CLF) recently catalogued 12 such policy actions in its newly released Public Lands […]

mix_items.title: Cyclone batters India’s eastern coast, killing 3 and damaging homes and farmland
mix_items.summary: KAKINADA, India (AP) — A powerful cyclone battered India ’s Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday, killing at least three people and damaging homes and farmland after authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people, officials said. Cyclone Arnab made landfall early Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm before weakening to a severe cyclonic storm as […]

mix_items.title: Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
mix_items.summary: A major new study reveals that drinking just two alcoholic beverages a day is associated with a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of death from alcohol-related causes, challenging the idea that moderate drinking is harmless. Researchers also found no significant overall health benefits from alcohol, with risks rising as consumption increases.

mix_items.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
mix_items.summary: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

mix_items.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
mix_items.summary: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.

mix_items.title: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage.

mix_items.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
mix_items.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

mix_items.title: The new certification scheme helping solar farms become havens for wildlife
mix_items.summary: A new solar certification scheme encourages developers to create better habitats for wildlife alongside clean electricity generation The post The new certification scheme helping solar farms become havens for wildlife appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
mix_items.summary: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.

mix_items.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
mix_items.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

mix_items.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
mix_items.summary: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

mix_items.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
mix_items.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.
